x: Brass is Cu + Zn, duralumin Al + Cu + Mg + Mn, amalgam is mercury with another metal and nichrome is Ni + Cr, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.

x: Option C is incorrect: sterling silver is 92.5% silver and 7.5% copper, not the reverse. The stainless steel, German silver and solder compositions are right.
t: Check percentages for a reversal.

x: Both are true and R explains A: high resistivity turns current into heat, and a high melting point and oxidation resistance let it glow red-hot without burning out.
t: Check whether R is the reason for the use in A.

x: Statement A is true: bronze is hard, corrosion-resistant, non-sparking and rings well. Statement B is false: solder's key property is its low melting point.
t: Recall the key property of each alloy.

x: Statements I, II and IV are keyed correct: steel is strong, duralumin light and strong, and brass golden. III is also true, as amalgam is soft when mixed and then sets, but no option lists all four.
t: Check each statement; note when the options leave out a true one.

x: Alnico makes permanent magnets, gunmetal guns, bearings and valves, amalgam dental fillings and duralumin aircraft parts, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the use of each alloy.

x: Three are copper alloys: brass, bronze and German silver. Alnico is an iron alloy with aluminium, nickel and cobalt.
t: Recall the base metal of each alloy.

x: Stainless steel resists rust thanks to chromium, so it is used in utensils, surgical tools, buildings, cars and aircraft. Brass and duralumin have narrower uses.
t: Recall the uses of stainless steel.

x: Bronze is copper with tin. Copper with zinc is brass, iron with carbon is steel and lead, antimony and tin is type metal.
t: Discriminate bronze (Cu + Sn) from brass (Cu + Zn).

x: Steel is Fe + C, lead-free solder Sn + Ag + Cu, bell metal Cu + Sn and type metal Pb + Sb + Sn, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the make-up of each alloy.

x: All three are correct: gunmetal is Cu + Sn + Zn, bell metal is bronze rich in tin, and copper is the base of gunmetal.
t: Recall the copper–tin alloys.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the name nickel silver comes from its nickel content and silvery look, not from zinc.
t: Check whether R explains the name.

x: Both are true: nickel is in German silver (Cu + Ni + Zn) and in alnico (Al + Ni + Co + Fe).
t: Recall the alloys containing nickel.

x: Iron forms steel, silver forms sterling silver, and lead is in both solder and type metal, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the alloys of each metal.

x: Brass is harder and more corrosion-resistant than pure copper, which is why it is used in fittings. Carbon-dependent hardness is steel, and chromium resistance is stainless steel.
t: Discriminate the features of brass, steel and stainless steel.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the 2% limit only defines steel, while hardness changes because different amounts of carbon change the structure.
t: Check whether R explains A or only defines a limit.

x: Stainless steel resists rust because of chromium, solder joins metals easily, German silver is hard, and dental amalgam uses silver, tin or copper with mercury, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the key property of each alloy.

x: All three are correct: German silver is tough, corrosion-resistant and silvery, though it contains no silver.
t: Recall the properties of German silver.

x: Option A is incorrect: nichrome has a high melting point, which suits heating elements. It also resists oxidation and has high resistivity.
t: Recall why nichrome is used in heaters.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: sterling silver is harder because of its 7.5% copper; keeping its lustre is a separate property.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: Brass is used in utensils, fittings and instruments, bronze in bells, sculpture and coins, and steel in buildings, vehicles and defence, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Recall the use of each alloy.

x: Both are true: solder joins metals and makes electrical connections because it melts at a low temperature.
t: Recall the uses of solder.

x: Both are true: solder is used in electronics and plumbing, and German silver in cutlery, marine fittings and electrical parts.
t: Recall the uses of each alloy.

x: Three are nichrome uses: toasters, heaters and furnaces. Plumbing fixtures use German silver or brass.
t: Recall the uses of nichrome.

x: All four are sterling-silver uses: jewellery, silverware, decorations and luxury goods.
t: Recall the uses of sterling silver.

x: All five are correct: brass is used in hardware and plumbing, and bronze in medals, statues and bearings.
t: Recall the uses of brass and bronze.

x: German silver is used in tableware, marine fittings and, because of its resistance, heating coils. Fillings use amalgam, aircraft duralumin and magnets alnico.
t: Recall the uses of each alloy.

x: CaSO₄·½H₂O is Plaster of Paris. Gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O, quicklime CaO and bleaching powder CaOCl₂.
t: Discriminate hemihydrate (Plaster of Paris) from dihydrate (gypsum).

x: Option B is incorrect: magnetite (Fe₃O₄) is the magnetic oxide of iron, while haematite is Fe₂O₃. The bauxite, galena and cryolite descriptions are right.
t: Discriminate haematite from magnetite.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the formula D₂O only names it, while heavy water moderates because deuterium slows neutrons without absorbing them.
t: Check whether R explains the use or only the identity.

x: Both are true: deuterium is ²H, written D, and oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust at about 46.6%.
t: Recall the abundance order: O, Si, Al, Fe.

x: Aluminium comes from bauxite and cryolite, iron from haematite and magnetite, copper from chalcopyrite and cuprite, and zinc from zinc blende and smithsonite, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the ores of each metal.

x: I and II are correct: brass is Cu + Zn and bronze Cu + Sn. III is false because German silver is Cu + Ni + Zn with no silver.
t: Recall that German silver has no silver.

x: Water gas is CO + H₂, made by passing steam over red-hot coke. He + O₂ is heliox and HCl + HNO₃ is aqua regia.
t: Recall the make-up of fuel gases.

x: Both are true and R explains A: pH 7 is the neutral point, so pure water at pH 7 is neutral.
t: Check whether R is the rule behind A.

x: Solid CO₂ is dry ice, N₂O laughing gas, PTFE Teflon and sulphur brimstone, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the common names of chemicals.

x: Two are sulphides: galena (PbS) and cinnabar (HgS). Smithsonite is a carbonate and cassiterite an oxide.
t: Classify ores by their anion.

x: C₆₀ is buckminsterfullerene, called a buckyball because it looks like a football. Brimstone is sulphur and the stranger gas is xenon.
t: Recall the common names of chemicals.

x: CaO is quicklime, hydrated magnesium silicate is talc, xenon is the "stranger" gas and sulphur is brimstone, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the common names of chemicals.

x: Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate, CaSO₄·2H₂O. The hemihydrate is Plaster of Paris.
t: Discriminate gypsum from Plaster of Paris.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the 3:1 HCl–HNO₃ mix produces chlorine species that oxidise gold and complex it, which neither acid can do alone.
t: Check whether R is the reason for A.

x: Lead comes from galena, mercury from cinnabar, silver from argentite and tin from cassiterite, giving a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the ore of each metal.

x: Sodium comes from rock salt, potassium from sylvine and carnallite, magnesium from magnesite and dolomite, and calcium from limestone and gypsum, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall the ores of alkali and alkaline earth metals.

x: Heliox is a diving gas, a carat is 200 mg of gem weight, a karat measures gold purity, and aqua regia is 3:1 HCl and HNO₃, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Discriminate carat (gem weight) from karat (gold purity).

x: All three are correct: hydrogen has protium, deuterium and tritium, carbon forms graphite, diamond, fullerene and graphene, and helium is a noble gas.
t: Recall the isotopes and allotropes of elements.

x: I and II are correct: fluorine is the most reactive halogen, and bromine is the only liquid non-metal. III is false because iodine is a solid.
t: Recall the states of the halogens.

x: Both are true: nitrogen makes up about 78% of air, and fluorine is the most reactive halogen.
t: Recall basic element facts.

x: Statement A is true: platinum and palladium occur native as noble metals. Statement B is false: chlorine, not xenon, is used to purify water.
t: Recall the use of each element.

x: Two contain aluminium: duralumin (Al, Cu, Mg, Mn) and alnico (Al, Ni, Co, Fe). Nichrome and solder have none.
t: Recall the make-up of each alloy.

x: All four contain nickel: German silver, stainless steel, nichrome and alnico.
t: Recall the make-up of each alloy.

x: Steel is iron with 0.1–2% carbon. Copper and zinc make brass and nickel and chromium nichrome.
t: Recall the make-up of steel.

x: Calcium hypochlorite is the active part of bleaching powder. Quicklime is CaO and talc is magnesium silicate.
t: Recall the common names of calcium compounds.

x: Hydrated magnesium silicate is talc or soapstone, the softest mineral. Calcite is CaCO₃ and corundum Al₂O₃.
t: Recall the common names of minerals.

x: N₂O is laughing gas, PTFE Teflon, xenon the stranger gas and sulphur brimstone, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the common names of chemicals.

x: Bauxite is Al₂O₃·xH₂O, cryolite Na₃AlF₆, haematite Fe₂O₃ and magnetite Fe₃O₄, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the xH₂O in Al₂O₃·xH₂O shows water is bound to the oxide, which is what hydrated means.
t: Check whether R shows A.

x: All four are correct: monazite is the thorium mineral, ilmenite the titanium mineral, rock salt the sodium mineral, and sylvine and carnallite the potassium minerals.
t: Recall the main mineral of each element.

x: Both are true: pearl is calcium carbonate bound with the protein conchiolin, and mercury forms amalgams with most metals except iron.
t: Recall the make-up of pearl and amalgam.

x: All four are correct: CaCO₃ is limestone, hydrated magnesium silicate talc, sodium thiosulphate hypo and Al₂O₃ corundum.
t: Recall the common names of chemicals.

x: Chlorine purifies water and is used to make tear gas. Aircraft and magnets use alloys, and methanol comes from water gas.
t: Recall the uses of chlorine.

x: Brass makes utensils and decorations, bronze coins, statues and bearings, duralumin aircraft and alnico magnets, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the use of each alloy.

x: All four are correct: gypsum is CaSO₄·2H₂O, cryolite Na₃AlF₆, pearl about 82–86% CaCO₃ as aragonite, and ruby and sapphire are Al₂O₃ with trace metals.
t: Recall the composition of minerals and gems.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the formula CO₂ shows dry ice is simply carbon dioxide in solid form.
t: Check whether R identifies A.

x: Heliox, helium mixed with oxygen, is breathed in deep-sea diving because helium does not cause nitrogen narcosis.
t: Recall the use of heliox.

x: Water gas (CO + H₂) is the feedstock for making methanol. Bleaching powder uses chlorine and Teflon uses tetrafluoroethylene.
t: Recall the uses of water gas.

x: Hydrogen is H, protium ¹H, tritium ³H and helium He, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.

x: The symbols are C for carbon, N for nitrogen, O for oxygen and F for fluorine, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Recall element symbols.

x: The symbols are Cl for chlorine, Br for bromine, I for iodine and Xe for xenon, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall element symbols.

x: All four are correct: calcium oxide is CaO, and calcite, marble and limestone are all forms of calcium carbonate.
t: Recall the forms of calcium carbonate.

x: Ruby and sapphire are corundum, aqua regia is the king of acids, quicklime is calcium and oxygen (CaO) and Plaster of Paris is calcined gypsum, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the common names of chemicals.

x: Monazite is a rare-earth phosphate (thorium source) and ilmenite is FeTiO₃, giving a-ii, b-i.
t: Recall India's beach-sand minerals.

x: Stainless steel is rust-free, steel is structural, solder joins metals and nichrome makes heating coils, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the use of each alloy.

x: Both are true: amalgam is used for dental fillings, and dry ice sublimes at −78.5°C.
t: Recall the facts about amalgam and dry ice.

x: Tin–lead solder is a soft solder, melting at low temperature. Duralumin is the aircraft alloy, alnico the magnet alloy and nichrome the heating alloy.
t: Recall the class of each alloy.

x: Stainless steel contains at least about 10–12% chromium, which forms a protective oxide film that stops rust.
t: Recall the role of chromium in stainless steel.

x: Calcium oxide is burnt lime, nitrous oxide N₂O, polytetrafluoroethylene PTFE and aluminium oxide Al₂O₃, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the names and formulas of chemicals.

x: Both are true: C₆₀ is called soccer-ball carbon, and limestone and marble are both CaCO₃.
t: Recall the common names of chemicals.

x: All four are correct: zinc blende is ZnS (zinc sulphide) and chalcopyrite is CuFeS₂ (copper iron sulphide).
t: Recall the formulas of sulphide ores.

x: Ruby and sapphire are Al₂O₃, laughing gas N₂O, Teflon (C₂F₄)ₙ and brass about 68–71% copper with zinc, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the formulas and compositions.

x: Both are true: bronze is about 88% copper and 12% tin, and German silver is about 50–60% copper with nickel and zinc.
t: Recall the percentages in copper alloys.

x: All four are correct: corundum is Al₂O₃, chalcopyrite CuFeS₂, cuprite Cu₂O and zinc blende ZnS.
t: Recall the formulas of ores.

x: Argentite is Ag₂S, rock salt NaCl, sylvine KCl and carnallite KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the formulas of ores.

x: Magnesite is MgCO₃. Dolomite is CaMg(CO₃)₂, limestone CaCO₃ and gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O.
t: Discriminate magnesite from dolomite.

x: Dolomite is the double carbonate CaMg(CO₃)₂. Magnesite is MgCO₃ alone.
t: Discriminate dolomite from magnesite.
